meta.name: Personal Admin Panel Standard
meta.purpose: A baseline set of functional features and UI conventions every admin/management section of any future project must include, regardless of the app's domain. This is a companion file to personal-design-standard.json — that file governs visual language (typography, color, signature elements); this file governs what the admin experience must functionally contain and how data-heavy screens should behave.
meta.relationship_to_design_standard: Every screen described here must still follow personal-design-standard.json for typography, color derivation, empty-state handling, and the anti_patterns list. Example violation caught in practice: an admin screenshot for a different project used a violet/indigo accent — that color is explicitly banned in personal-design-standard.json.anti_patterns. Apply both files together.

user_management_module.status: REQUIRED in every project that has more than one role or any concept of a login.

baseline_features.notes: Admin can create a user directly (set name, email, role, and any org-structure assignment like team/unit/department) rather than only supporting self-signup.
Optional alternative to direct creation — send an invite link/email that lets the person set their own password. Prefer this over admin-set temporary passwords when email is available.
Change name, email, role, org assignment after creation.

Soft-disable rather than hard-delete by default, so historical records (their past actions, submissions, etc.) stay intact. Deactivated users cannot log in; existing sessions/tokens are invalidated immediately on deactivation.
See account_security.lockout_policy — admin must be able to manually unlock an account that's been locked out from failed login attempts, not just wait for auto-expiry.
Admin can trigger a password reset (send reset link) for a user who's locked out or forgot their password. Admin should not be able to see or set a user's password in plaintext.
Role changes take effect immediately; if the app uses stateless tokens (JWT), the change should be reflected on next request via a role check against the DB, not just trusted from a stale token.
Each user row shows last login timestamp at minimum, so an admin can spot accounts that have never logged in (stuck invites) or gone stale.
By name/email at minimum; by role and status (active/deactivated/locked) where the user list is large enough to need it.

lockout_policy.trigger: Lock the account after N consecutive failed login attempts (default suggestion: 5).
lockout_policy.auto_unlock: Optionally auto-unlock after a cooldown window (e.g. 15–30 minutes) so a genuine user isn't permanently stuck without admin involvement.
lockout_policy.manual_unlock: Admin can always manually unlock immediately, regardless of the cooldown — this must be a visible, one-click action on the user's row/profile, not buried in a settings page.
lockout_policy.visibility: A locked account must be visually distinguishable in the user list (a status badge, per personal-design-standard.json badge conventions — color plus text label, never color alone).

password_and_session_rules: Passwords are always stored hashed (never plaintext, never reversible encryption).
Deactivating a user immediately invalidates their active sessions/tokens — they should not be able to keep using the app until a token naturally expires.
Role changes and deactivation should be checked against current DB state on protected requests, not solely trusted from a token's claims if the token has a long lifetime.

roles_and_permissions_baseline.principle: Every project defines roles explicitly (even a 2-role project: admin + user) and documents what each role can see/do, mirroring the pattern used in a project's own spec (roles + permissions list). Do not leave permission boundaries implicit in code with no documented source of truth.
roles_and_permissions_baseline.superadmin_or_top_role_expectations: Whatever the top-level role is called (admin, superadmin, owner), it must be able to: manage all users (per user_management_module), view system-wide data, and manage the org-structure entities the app is built around (e.g. teams/departments/categories/projects — whatever the app's core grouping concept is).

required_elements: Column headers that are always visible (sticky if the list scrolls).
Row-level actions (edit, deactivate, view detail) either inline or via a row menu — never require navigating away just to see what actions exist.
Search/filter bar above any list expected to exceed ~15-20 rows.
Pagination or infinite scroll once a list can realistically grow past one screen — decide which up front rather than shipping neither.

empty_states.rule: A table with zero rows must never render as a bare header with dead space below it (see the AssetPulse Categories screenshot for the failure mode: header row, then nothing). It must show a clear message plus the primary action to fix it, e.g. 'No categories yet — create your first one' with the create button restated inline, not just relying on the button already in the page header.
empty_states.rationale: An empty table with no guidance reads as broken, not as 'nothing here yet'. This is the single most common admin-UI mistake and is explicitly disallowed.

navigation.breadcrumbs: Any nested admin screen (e.g. Section / Subsection) shows a breadcrumb trail, consistent with however the rest of the app's information architecture is described in that project's own spec.
navigation.active_state: The current section is visually distinguished in the nav (per personal-design-standard.json's accent-color rules — used deliberately, not as a wash).

forms_within_admin.rule: Creation/edit forms follow personal-design-standard.json's forms section (labels above inputs, inline validation) — no separate rule needed here, just confirming it applies to admin CRUD forms specifically, which is where it's most often skipped in practice.

bulk_actions.when_required: Once a list is expected to regularly exceed ~10 items an admin might act on together (e.g. deactivate 5 users at once), support multi-select plus a bulk action bar. Not required for lists that are inherently small (e.g. a company's list of Groups, capped at a handful).

admin_ui_conventions.confirmation_for_destructive_actions: Any action that deletes data or removes access (delete, deactivate, revoke) requires an explicit confirmation step (dialog or type-to-confirm for the most destructive ones) — never a single click with no confirmation.

audit_and_activity.minimum_bar: Even without a full audit log module, every admin-manageable entity (users, and whatever the project's core entities are) should track created_at and, where the entity can be modified, an updated_at timestamp. This is the cheap baseline; a full activity/audit feed (who did what, when) is a project-by-project decision, not a mandatory baseline — evaluate per project whether compliance/accountability needs justify it.

process_checklist.instructions: Run through when scaffolding the admin/management side of any new project.
steps: 1. Define roles explicitly, even if there are only two.

2. Scaffold the User Management screen with every feature in user_management_module.baseline_features — create, invite, edit, deactivate/reactivate, unlock, reset password, role assignment, last-login visibility, search/filter.
3. Implement lockout_policy: failed-attempt threshold, optional auto-unlock cooldown, and a one-click manual unlock for admins.

4. For every data table/list in the admin area: confirm pagination-or-infinite-scroll is decided, and write the empty state copy before shipping — do not leave a table that can legitimately render with zero rows without one.
5. Add confirmation steps to every destructive action.

6. Cross-check every admin screen against personal-design-standard.json (typography, color derivation, anti_patterns) — admin screens are exactly where generic dark-dashboard defaults tend to creep back in.
